title: Delhi, 1783
hookLine: Baghel Singh camped at Delhi and marked the sites where gurdwaras like Sis Ganj now stand

lines: HE ASKS FOR THE GURUS' PLACES.
cards: A Sikh army is camped outside Delhi, the seat of the Mughal emperors. The court is nervous. The army's leader, Baghel Singh, could ask for a great deal: money, land, a share of the city's wealth.

The court wants him gone. Tradition says that along with a share of the city's taxes, he asked for something stranger: to stay a while, and to find and mark the places in the city where the Gurus had been.

teach.h: THE GURU WAS KILLED IN DELHI.
teach.b: Why Delhi? Guru Tegh Bahadur was put to death there, in the middle of the city; Sikhs remember it as the price of standing up for other people's freedom to worship. Sikhs knew roughly where.
But the city had moved on, and shops, houses and other buildings stood on ground Sikhs remembered as sacred.
Tradition says Baghel Singh set about finding the exact spots: where the Guru was beheaded, where his body was secretly cremated, where other Gurus had stayed.
Some of it, tradition says, came down to asking people who remembered. Then the places were marked, so that gurdwaras could rise there. The name you can still find on a map of Delhi is Sis Ganj.
Sis is an old word for head, still used in Punjabi.

teach.h: SIS GANJ: WHERE HE GAVE HIS HEAD.
teach.b: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib stands in Chandni Chowk, a crowded old market street, on the place Sikhs remember as where the Guru gave his head.
There's a deeper day on this path later for the Guru's death itself; today's story is the marking. Armies come and go, and their camps are forgotten. The gurdwaras he marked still draw people in.

teach.h: A MEMORY GIVEN A PLACE TO LIVE.
teach.b: He used his one moment of power to make sure a memory had a place to live.

how: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, is visited by Sikhs and others; Baghel Singh's role in marking Delhi's Sikh sites is told in Sikh histories.

practice: If there's a gurdwara near you, you can go in any day; anyone is welcome, with head covered and shoes off.

If not, picture one: shoes left at the door, a cloth over your hair, the Guru Granth Sahib under its canopy, someone singing; sit at the back, in your mind or for real, and notice that this room stands on a spot someone chose to remember.
If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Delhi. Tradition says Baghel Singh, camped at the capital, found and marked the places where the Gurus had been, so that gurdwaras like Sis Ganj could stand there. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for Sis Ganj; sis means head, and the gurdwara marks where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded.
